summary.text: Define an auxiliary sequence by \(r_0=-2\), \(r_1=-56\), and \(r_{n+2}=-4r_{n+1}-64r_n\). Algebra shows that both \(r_n^2\) and the odd-indexed terms satisfy \(x_{n+3}=-48x_{n+2}+3072x_{n+1}+262144x_n\); matching the first three values and induction give \(a(2n+1)=r_n^2\).

full_proof.text:
Let \((a_n)_{n\ge 0}\) be the integer sequence defined by
\[
a_0=-1,\qquad a_1=4,\qquad a_2=176,\qquad a_3=3136,
\]
and, for every \(k\ge 0\),
\[
a_{k+4}=-4a_{k+3}+256a_{k+1}+4096a_k.
\]
We prove that every odd-indexed term \(a_{2n+1}\) is a square of an integer.

First we derive a recurrence involving terms whose indices differ by two. For every \(k\ge 0\), apply the defining recurrence at indices \(k+6\) and \(k+5\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{k+6}
&=-4a_{k+5}+256a_{k+3}+4096a_{k+2},\\
a_{k+5}
&=-4a_{k+4}+256a_{k+2}+4096a_{k+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Substituting the second equality into the first gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{k+6}
&=-4\bigl(-4a_{k+4}+256a_{k+2}+4096a_{k+1}\bigr)
  +256a_{k+3}+4096a_{k+2}\\
&=16a_{k+4}+3072a_{k+2}+256a_{k+3}-16384a_{k+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
On the other hand, the defining recurrence at index \(k+4\) says
\[
a_{k+4}=-4a_{k+3}+256a_{k+1}+4096a_k.
\]
Multiplying this identity by \(-64\) and rearranging yields
\[
256a_{k+3}-16384a_{k+1}=-64a_{k+4}+262144a_k.
\]
Using this in the preceding expression for \(a_{k+6}\), we obtain
\[
\boxed{a_{k+6}=-48a_{k+4}+3072a_{k+2}+262144a_k.}
\tag{1}
\]
Thus, after restricting to indices of one parity, the original fourth-order recurrence becomes a three-term recurrence.

We now construct the integers whose squares will be the odd-indexed terms. Define an auxiliary integer sequence \((r_n)_{n\ge 0}\) by
\[
r_0=-2,\qquad r_1=-56,
\]
and
\[
r_{n+2}=-4r_{n+1}-64r_n\qquad(n\ge 0).
\tag{2}
\]
We claim that the squares \(r_n^2\) obey the same recurrence as the odd-indexed subsequence of \(a\). More precisely, for every \(n\ge 0\),
\[
\boxed{r_{n+3}^2=-48r_{n+2}^2+3072r_{n+1}^2+262144r_n^2.}
\tag{3}
\]
To prove this identity, put \(x=r_n\) and \(y=r_{n+1}\). By (2),
\[
r_{n+2}=-4y-64x.
\]
Applying (2) once more gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
r_{n+3}
&=-4r_{n+2}-64r_{n+1}\\
&=-4(-4y-64x)-64y\\
&=256x-48y.
\end{aligned}
\]
Consequently,
\[
r_{n+3}^2=(256x-48y)^2
=65536x^2-24576xy+2304y^2.
\tag{4}
\]
Meanwhile,
\[
\begin{aligned}
&-48r_{n+2}^2+3072r_{n+1}^2+262144r_n^2\\
&\quad=-48(-4y-64x)^2+3072y^2+262144x^2\\
&\quad=-48\bigl(16y^2+512xy+4096x^2\bigr)
       +3072y^2+262144x^2\\
&\quad=2304y^2-24576xy+65536x^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
This is the expression in (4), proving (3).

We next establish the stronger exact identity
\[
\boxed{a_{2n+1}=r_n^2\quad\text{for every }n\ge 0.}
\tag{5}
\]
The first three cases are checked directly.

For \(n=0\),
\[
a_1=4=(-2)^2=r_0^2.
\]
For \(n=1\),
\[
a_3=3136=(-56)^2=r_1^2.
\]
For the case \(n=2\), first calculate the needed terms of \(a\) from its defining recurrence:
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_4
&=-4a_3+256a_1+4096a_0\\
&=-4(3136)+256(4)+4096(-1)\\
&=-15616,
\end{aligned}
\]
and hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_5
&=-4a_4+256a_2+4096a_1\\
&=-4(-15616)+256(176)+4096(4)\\
&=123904.
\end{aligned}
\]
The auxiliary recurrence gives
\[
r_2=-4r_1-64r_0=-4(-56)-64(-2)=352,
\]
and
\[
r_2^2=352^2=123904=a_5.
\]
Thus (5) holds for \(n=0,1,2\).

Now suppose \(m\ge 0\), and assume that (5) is already known at the three consecutive indices \(m,m+1,m+2\); that is,
\[
a_{2m+1}=r_m^2,
\qquad
a_{2(m+1)+1}=r_{m+1}^2,
\qquad
a_{2(m+2)+1}=r_{m+2}^2.
\tag{6}
\]
Apply the step-six recurrence (1) with \(k=2m+1\). This gives
\[
a_{2m+7}=-48a_{2m+5}+3072a_{2m+3}+262144a_{2m+1}.
\]
Since
\[
2m+7=2(m+3)+1,\quad
2m+5=2(m+2)+1,\quad
2m+3=2(m+1)+1,
\]
the induction hypotheses (6) transform this equality into
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{2(m+3)+1}
&=-48r_{m+2}^2+3072r_{m+1}^2+262144r_m^2\\
&=r_{m+3}^2,
\end{aligned}
\]
where the last equality is precisely the square recurrence (3). Therefore (5) at the indices \(m,m+1,m+2\) implies (5) at index \(m+3\). Together with the three initial cases, induction proves (5) for every nonnegative integer \(n\).

Finally, each \(r_n\) is an integer, so (5) explicitly writes the odd-indexed term as the square of an integer:
\[
a_{2n+1}=r_n^2.
\]
Hence \(a(2n+1)\) is a perfect square for every nonnegative integer \(n\), as required.
